newsitem.title: FRANCE: France renews appeal for Zaire ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: France renews appeal for Zaire ceasefire.

text.p: France renewed appeals on Tuesday to Tutsi rebels sweeping across eastern Zaire to agree to a ceasefire as a senior U.S. official visited Paris for talks on ways to defuse the crisis.
"It is important that all the parties involved, the leaders of the rebellion and the countries which back them, immediately accept a ceasefire," Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said.
He said that the Kinshasa government had already backed a U.N. ceasefire plan foreseeing talks, elections and an international conference on the crisis.

"Only the start of talks after such a ceasefire will enable us to avoid a destabilisation of Zaire with unpredictable consequences," he told a routine briefing. "All the international community should mobilise efforts in this direction."
Doutriaux said U.S. Assistant Secretary of State George Moose was in Paris on Tuesday for talks on Zaire with Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and officials at President Jacques Chirac's office.
"France and the United States must have a very close cooperation on the subject of Zaire," he said.

France has long backed ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, 66 despite opposition charges of rampant corruption under his three decades in power. It has urged sending troops to help refugees, a plan opposed by Washington.
Mobutu, who has spent most of his time on the French Riviera since surgery for prostate cancer last year, was readmitted to hospital in Monaco at the weekend.
Zaire accuses English-speaking Uganda and its Tutsi allies in Rwanda and Burundi of backing the rebels. The three countries deny the charges.

Rebel chief Laurent Kabila, with little interest in a general ceasefire while his troops seem to be gaining the upper hand, vowed on Tuesday that his forces would take over Africa's third largest country.

He promised a temporary ceasefire for 20 km (13 miles) around the newly captured city of Kisangani to allow in humanitarian aid and let people who fled return, but said advances on all other fronts would continue.
